endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Future risk predictions require 1-2 years of available data.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Given the newness of AI and its potential for clinically significant effects on care, equitable accountability must be established.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: The Disease X screening model is software intended to aid in screening for Disease X on patients 2038 above the age of 22 by analyzing 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recorded from compatible 2039 ECG devices.

endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: It involves defining the intended and unintended use, constraints, and the target population for the solution.

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: Also includes guides for preventing inappropriate use of AI products beyond their intended scope.

endorsements.title: A normative framework for artificial intelligence as a sociotechnical system in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Use parameters and limitations: a specification of the conditions within which the system can be used to achieve such benchmarks and outside of which its performance is expected to degrade, along with protocols or practices for implementing the system within these conditions under real-world conditions.

endorsements.title: The selective deployment of AI in healthcare: An ethical algorithm for algorithms
endorsements.quote: Selective deployment: System developers can release an algorithm for patient subgroups where the model performs well, while withholding the algorithm from those patient subgroups for whom the model is expected to perform poorly (or unpredictably).

endorsements.title: Traffic Light Coding System for Engaging With AI in Surgery
endorsements.quote: Therefore, clinicians must treat AI‐based devices like any other medical device and ensure their use is consistent with the intended purpose it was approved for.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Drafting of Chest X-Ray Reports: 2025 Position Statement From the Korean Society of Thoracic Radiology Based on an Expert Survey
endorsements.quote: The thoracic radiologists judged the tool to be suitable only for screening examinations reviewed by a radiologist.

endorsements.title: AI Scribe Use in Residency Training: A Call for Specialty Society Guidance in Graduate Medical Education
endorsements.issuer: Advances in medical education and practice
endorsements.quote: Such policies should incorporate mandatory resident review and note sign-off of AI-generated notes, clear accountability protocols, patient consent standards, and limitations on use depending on the note section such as formulation of assessment and plan.

endorsements.title: A Clinical-Operational Framework for Responsible Artificial Intelligence Use in Infection Risk Management Among Immunosuppressed Patients: A Technical Report
endorsements.quote: Local validation before clinical use and restriction to the approved purpose

endorsements.title: A six-level clinical autonomy framework for artificial intelligence in dentistry
endorsements.quote: Here, the COD defines the validated boundary of operation (setting, patient category, procedure scope, modality availability, contraindications, and reversibility window).

endorsements.title: An evidence informed framework for artificial intelligence in rare breast cancers using small cohort validation synthetic data practices and clinical governance
endorsements.quote: Practice point: deployment dossiers should state the maximum safe scope of use and list contraindications, including untested subtypes, unscreened populations or unsupported workflows.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing AI-Enabled Cardiovascular Biomarkers: A Clinician-Centered Framework for Validation, Governance, and Workflow Integration
endorsements.quote: Its intended use must remain narrow: the output is a screening prompt for confirmatory assessment, not a diagnosis of heart failure or an independent indication for treatment.

evidence.title: Structural Findings Transfer, Texture Findings Do Not: An Adaptation Ladder for Cross-Center Dental Diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Whether an out-of-distribution gate refuses inputs from an unseen center instead of predicting unreliably
evidence.effect: Mahalanobis OOD gate over frozen embeddings acts as a directional shift detector; a gate re-fit on the target defers about five percent there regardless of technique; guarantee never breaks across 126 configurations.
evidence.quote: The refusal gate is a directional distribution-shift detector—a gate re-fit on the target defers about five percent there regardless of technique—so refusal reflects calibration, not adaptation strength.
evidence.sample_unit: adaptation configurations (10 techniques x budgets x 3 backbones)

evidence.title: False Positives in Artificial Intelligence Prioritization Software for Intracranial Hemorrhage Identification in the Postoperative Period: A Report of Two Cases
evidence.outcome: False-positive ICH flags by AI prioritization software on postoperative CT
evidence.effect: Two cases in which AI prioritization software erroneously identified an acute ICH on a postoperative non-contrast CT.
evidence.quote: However, it is crucial to recognize that AI systems may produce false-positive results, especially in the postoperative period.

evidence.title: Efficacy of an Automated Pulmonary Embolism (PE) Detection Algorithm on Routine Contrast-Enhanced Chest CT Imaging for Non-PE Studies
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Performance of PE AI when applied to non-dedicated CT studies outside its intended use
evidence.effect: On non-dedicated contrast-enhanced chest CTs, sensitivity was only 0.14 (specificity 1.00), versus 41% overall sensitivity.
evidence.quote: The predictions for non-dedicated contrast-enhanced chest CT imaging studies were 90.48% accurate, with a sensitivity of 0.14 and specificity of 1.00.
evidence.sample_unit: contrast-enhanced chest CT exams (130 dedicated, 63 non-dedicated)

evidence.title: AI in the Shadows: Unveiling the Strengths and Blind Spots of Medios AI Retinal Screening in Cancer Care
evidence.outcome: AI performance when applied to oncology patients outside its intended DR/ARMD/glaucoma screening population
evidence.effect: Eight patients with leukemic retinopathy were incorrectly flagged as having DR; optic atrophy was not detected; AI correct for glaucoma (3), DR (2), ARMD (2).
evidence.quote: However, eight patients with leukemic retinopathy were incorrectly flagged as having DR, revealing a lack of specificity in distinguishing vascular retinal pathologies.

evidence.title: Performance of an Adult-Trained AI Algorithm for Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection on Pediatric Head CT
evidence.outcome: Adult-trained AI performance when applied to pediatric patients aged 6-17 (off-population use)
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 94.2% (95% CI 89.6-97.2), specificity 94.7%, accuracy 94.6%, NPV 99.4%, PPV 62.5%; comparable to adult performance, though prospective validation is required.
evidence.quote: An adult-trained AI algorithm demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy for ICH detection in pediatric patients aged 6–17 years, comparable to its adult performance.

evidence.title: Consecutive prediction of adverse maternal outcomes of preeclampsia, using the PIERS-ML and fullPIERS models: A multicountry prospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Performance of models used outside intended initial-assessment use (repeated use past 48 h)
evidence.effect: PIERS-ML performance declined notably for most risk groups beyond 48 h; fullPIERS AUC-PRC (0.2-0.4) close to daily fraction of adverse outcomes, indicating low discriminative capacity.
evidence.quote: We recommend using the models for consecutive prediction with greater caution and interpreting predictions with increasing uncertainty as the pregnancy progresses.
evidence.country: Multicountry (Americas, sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Europe, Oceania)

evidence.title: Deep learning for pediatric chest x-ray diagnosis: Repurposing a commercial tool developed for adults
evidence.outcome: Performance of adult-trained tool applied to pediatric population outside intended use
evidence.effect: Overall AUC 0.94 (sens 87.5%, spec 82.3%, PPV 56.6%) in children 2-14, but significantly lower in ages 2-6 (AUC 0.91) than 7-14 (AUC 0.96), p<0.001.
evidence.quote: In the older age group (n = 449 [46.9%]; mean age 10.2 ± 2 years), the performance metrics were as follows: AUC 0.96 (95% CI: 0.94–0.98), accuracy 89.7% (95% CI: 86.5–92.4%), sensitivity 86.2%, specificity 90.3%, PPV 56.8% and NPV 97.8%, respectively, which were significantly higher compared to the younger age groups (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: New frontiers in radiologic interpretation: evaluating the effectiveness of large language models in pneumothorax diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Performance in pediatric patients versus adults when applied outside validated population
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy in patients aged ≤12 years was 20.8%, 12.5%, and 20.8% versus 57.4-69.6% in adults across the three models.
evidence.quote: Performance was significantly poorer in pediatric patients across all models (20.8%, 12.5%, and 20.8%, respectively).

evidence.title: Head-to-Head Comparison of 2 Artificial Intelligence Tools for Detecting Lymph Node Metastases in Whole-Slide Pathology Images Within and Beyond Their Intended Use
evidence.venue: Modern pathology : an official journal of the United States and Canadian Academy of Pathology, Inc
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of AI tools on tumor types beyond their intended use
evidence.effect: Both tools showed excellent sensitivity for macrometastases across tumor types, including beyond intended use. DPL had slightly higher sensitivity for micrometastases and isolated tumor cells than VMD, particularly in lung cancer and melanoma.
evidence.quote: Our findings suggest that a single AI tool may be suitable for LN metastasis detection across multiple tumor types, even beyond its intended use.
evidence.sample_unit: patients with lymph node metastases (whole-slide images); plus 1012 tumor-negative slides for false-positive alerts

evidence.title: Robustness of a convolutional neural network trained on dermoscopic images and challenged with close-up images
evidence.venue: Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft = Journal of the German Society of Dermatology : JDDG
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of dermoscopy-trained CNN on close-up images, a setting it was not validated for
evidence.effect: Sensitivity fell from 88.2% (dermoscopic) to 60.5% (close-up, p < 0.001); specificity rose from 69.0% to 79.4% (p = 0.027); ROC-AUC 0.866 vs 0.780 (p = 0.003).
evidence.quote: For close-up images of the same lesions, sensitivity decreased to 60.5% (53.5%-67.1%, p < 0.001), while specificity increased to 79.4% (72.3%-85.0%, p = 0.027).

evidence.title: Performance of an adult-trained AI tool for intracranial hemorrhage detection on head CT in children aged 6-17 years
evidence.outcome: Performance of adult-trained ICH AI tool applied to pediatric patients aged 6-17
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 94.2% (162/172), specificity 94.7%, accuracy 94.6%, PPV 62.5%, NPV 99.4%; performance comparable to adult performance, though false positives were common.
evidence.quote: An adult-trained AI tool demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy for ICH detection in pediatric patients aged 6-17 years, comparable to its adult performance.

evidence.title: TotalSegmentator-AI for aortic segmentation in CT: Reliable performance in normal anatomy but limited utility in pathological aortic disease
evidence.outcome: Segmentation quality across normal versus pathological aortic anatomy categories
evidence.effect: Quality varied by category (p<0.001): best in young patients (median 5), poorest in dissections (median 3) and aneurysms (median 4); overall median 4, 77% good or excellent.
evidence.quote: Performance was consistent across segments (p = 0.16) but varied by category (p < 0.001): best in young patients (5 [IQR 4-5]) and adequate in non-contrast and venous-phase scans (4 [IQR 4-5]), poorest in dissections (3 [IQR 3-4]) and aneurysms (4 [IQR 3-4]).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Quantification of Longitudinal HRCT Changes During Treatment of Pulmonary Tuberculosis: An Exploratory Proof-of-Concept Study
evidence.outcome: Fit of a general lung-texture tool to tuberculosis HRCT, including cavity classification
evidence.effect: The software has no dedicated cavity class. Tuberculous cavities and post-destructive abnormalities were frequently labeled as emphysema. The abstract reports no quantitative error rate.
evidence.quote: As a result, emphysema-labeled low-attenuation areas should not be interpreted as conventional emphysema alone, because tuberculous cavities and post-destructive abnormalities were frequently included in this category.

evidence.title: Evaluating an AI-assisted triage workflow for retinal diseases
evidence.outcome: False negatives from out-of-distribution or atypical pathology outside the AI's target disease scope
evidence.effect: Composite false negatives included myopic chorioretinal atrophy, geographic atrophy, and treatment-altered DR; AI negatives were appropriate within scope but missed out-of-distribution pathology.
evidence.quote: While such classifications were appropriate within the algorithm’s defined scope, this discrepancy highlights a potential limitation of disease-specific AI models in negative-screening workflows, particularly when encountering out-of-distribution retinal pathologies.

evidence.title: ARE LLMS READY FOR PEDIATRICS? A COMPARATIVE EVALUATION OF MODEL ACCURACY ACROSS CLINICAL DOMAINS
evidence.outcome: Performance of general-purpose LLMs on pediatric content, a specialized population not specifically validated
evidence.effect: Five of eight LLMs performed significantly worse on pediatric than adult questions (up to more than 10 percentage points lower); three newer models performed comparably across domains.
evidence.quote: Five models (Amazon Nova Pro 1.0, GPT 3.5-turbo-0125, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Grok 2, and Claude 3 Sonnet) demonstrated significantly lower performance on pediatric questions, with accuracy drops of up to more than 10 percentage points.

evidence.title: The pediatric transfer gap: How adult-ICU-trained machine-learning models degrade on pediatric intensive care patients
evidence.outcome: Model performance when applied outside validated population
evidence.effect: Models trained on adults or older children lost discrimination and were miscalibrated in younger children, worst in neonates.
evidence.quote: Vital-sign-based mortality models trained on older children or directly observed adult-ICU data lose discrimination and become severely miscalibrated when applied to younger children, with neonates worst affected.

commentary.bottom_line: One automated benchmark suggests that an out-of-distribution gate can defer inputs from an unseen center, but no study tests inclusion criteria or workflow controls in clinical use. Fifteen hazard studies show that tools often lose accuracy outside their validated population or setting, which supports the concern without showing that such controls correct it.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a level 5 automated benchmark across 126 adaptation configurations, with no patients or clinicians involved. It reports that a Mahalanobis gate re-fit on the target deferred about five percent of inputs and that the guarantee held in every configuration. Indirectness and the absence of clinical outcomes place certainty at very low.

Pulmonary embolism sensitivity was 0.14 on non-dedicated CTs. Pediatric pneumothorax accuracy was 12.5 to 20.8% versus 57.4 to 69.6% in adults. Sensitivity fell from 88.2% to 60.5% on close-up skin images. Two pediatric head CT studies found performance comparable to adults, so harm from out-of-scope use may vary by tool.

Several failures arose from inputs the tool was not built for. These included postoperative head CTs, repeated model use past 48 hours, and pathology outside a fundus tool's target scope. Such cases suggest that controls would need to act at order entry or image routing. No study measures whether those controls work or what burden they add.

Several out-of-population failures involved children. Across 73,397 patients, models trained on adults or older children lost discrimination and were miscalibrated in younger children, worst in neonates. AUC was 0.91 in ages 2 to 6 versus 0.96 in ages 7 to 14. In India, eight oncology patients with leukemic retinopathy were flagged as having diabetic retinopathy. None reports Medicaid, safety-net, or language subgroups.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes intended use in terms of patient age and compatible recording devices. Several frameworks call for restriction to the approved purpose. No supplied study evaluates whether health-system enforcement of these labeled boundaries changes tool outputs or patient outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: No study tests whether defined inclusion and exclusion criteria, order-entry restrictions, or out-of-distribution gates reduce out-of-scope use or patient harm in live deployment. Prospective or stepped-wedge evaluations should measure how often tools are applied out of scope, how often controls block or defer those cases, how clinicians work around them, and what happens diagnostically to deferred patients.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test of the practice used benchmark data with no reported patient population. No hazard study reports Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Whether scope controls perform equally for these patients, or defer them at higher rates when they are underrepresented in training data, remains unknown.
